title: Linked Lists
summary: Rewire nodes with pointers, carefully, so nothing is lost or left in a cycle.
lesson:
How it works
- Each node holds a value and a reference to the next node; the list is reached only through its head.
- Inserting or removing after a known node is `O(1)`; finding the `k`th node is `O(k)`.
- There is no random access, so most algorithms walk the list once with a few pointer variables.

When to reach for it
- The input is already a linked list and you must rearrange it without copying values into an array.
- The question asks to reverse, merge, split, or reorder nodes.
- Constant extra space is required and an array copy would use `O(n)`.

Common patterns
- Dummy head: start the result at a placeholder node so the first real node needs no special case.
- Pointer reversal: keep `previous`, `current`, and `next` while turning each link around.
- Splicing: attach the chosen node to a tail pointer and advance it.
- Fast and slow pointers find the middle or detect a cycle.

Pitfalls
- Overwriting `current.next` before saving where it pointed; that loses the rest of the list.
- Returning the dummy node instead of `dummy.next`.
- Forgetting the empty list and the single-node list.
- Leaving an old link in place and creating a cycle.
